object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A declared or triaged event tracked in the incident system, identified by an incident number (INC-...). Never deleted once created.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.
Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for an incident, format INC- followed by a sequence.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A signal from the monitoring platform (or a manually-raised equivalent) that something may be wrong; can be an origin of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Monitoring fires an alert, or a customer tells us.
Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.
If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for an alert, sourced from the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A support ticket raised by or on behalf of a customer, which can be an origin of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for a support ticket, in a different format/system than incidents or alerts.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: Technical impact / blast radius classification of an incident, SEV1 (highest) to SEV4 (lowest).

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: Customer urgency classification of an incident, P1 (highest) to P4 (lowest), set by Support.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4.
Priority is about customer urgency.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The current lifecycle state of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.

object_types.name: Person
object_types.definition: An individual who can serve as incident commander for the duration of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: PersonName
object_types.definition: The name identifying a person acting as incident commander.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: A team that owns one or more services on a standing basis.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A catalogued service that can be affected by an incident and is owned by exactly one team.

ambiguities.description: Severity and Priority both appear mandatory only once an incident is 'declared'; are they also absent/optional during the 'triage' state like the commander? The transcript states severity is mandatory 'once declared' and priority is 'on every incident' but doesn't clarify if triage incidents have severity/priority at all.

source_references.excerpt: Every declared incident has a severity. That's mandatory, you can't declare without one. ... Priority too. Support sets it, and it's on every incident.

ambiguities.description: The internal_uniqueness constraint on 'Incident is duplicate of Incident' with roles ['Incident is duplicate of'] refers to the 'is duplicate of' role -- need clarity that this is the role played by the incident that IS a duplicate (the 'B' side), constraining it to at most one 'A' (primary).

source_references.excerpt: Can an incident be a duplicate of more than one other? ... No. One primary.

ambiguities.description: Is 'Alert has AlertId' internal uniqueness on the AlertId role (i.e., can one Alert ID map to multiple Alerts) actually verified, or just assumed by analogy to other identifiers? Not explicitly discussed for reuse/uniqueness the way Incident number was.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

ambiguities.description: Person identification: incident commander is described as 'named' but no explicit reference scheme (like employee ID) was discussed -- using PersonName as identifier may not be unique in reality (two people could share a name). Should there be an employee ID or similar unique identifier instead?

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

ambiguities.description: Team identification: 'Team' is identified by TeamName by inference, but the transcript never explicitly discusses team identifiers or their uniqueness -- only that services are owned by teams.

source_references.excerpt: A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

ambiguities.description: Severity history: severity changes are tracked in the timeline as events, but only the current severity is captured in the model. Should a temporal/historical severity-change fact type be modeled separately, since the transcript flags this as relevant 'later' but never resolves it?

source_references.excerpt: Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. ... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: Open business decision: whether incidents later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is is explicitly undecided and deferred to Ravi. No 'cause classification' concept exists in the current model, per explicit instruction, but this is a known gap for future modeling.

source_references.excerpt: Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided.

ambiguities.description: The 'monitoring' status Owen mentions is explicitly excluded from the model as it is not a real system state, but this reflects a gap between how people informally describe incident status ('monitoring') and the formal five-state model -- worth flagging as a potential future granularity/state issue.

source_references.excerpt: There's also "monitoring," which sits between mitigated and resolved. ... If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it. Five states.

ambiguities.description: Overloaded term 'owner': 'commander' and 'service owner' are both colloquially called 'owner' in conversation, causing ambiguity in communication (though the model itself distinguishes them clearly as separate fact types). Flagging to ensure downstream consumers don't conflate the two relationships.

source_references.excerpt: Now -- the other "owner." ... And in a channel, "who owns this?" means either. It's genuinely ambiguous every single time.

ambiguities.description: Overloaded term 'sev': people colloquially say 'sev' to mean either Severity or Priority, causing real-world miscommunication, though the two are modeled as distinct value types/fact types.

source_references.excerpt: And people say "sev" when they mean either.
